title: India's Stock Market Just Clawed Back to $5 Trillion. Here's What Turned the Tide.
excerpt: A 42% crash in oil prices, a steadier rupee, and a wave of RBI measures have brought global funds back to Indian equities after months of record outflows.
body:
India's stock market has reclaimed the $5 trillion equity valuation milestone, capping a remarkable turnaround after months of bruising volatility that had sent foreign investors fleeing and pushed the rupee to record lows.

The BSE Sensex closed at 77,155 on Wednesday, while the Nifty 50 ended at 24,086 — both at six-week highs. The rally has now stretched to four consecutive sessions, adding trillions of rupees in investor wealth and signalling a decisive shift in sentiment toward the world's fifth-largest economy.

What Changed

Two forces converged to reverse India's fortunes. Brent crude oil, which had surged past $126 a barrel in April after the US-Iran conflict erupted, has crashed 42% to trade below $71. For India — which imports nearly 90% of its crude — the drop is transformative. It eases the current account deficit, softens inflation, and frees up fiscal headroom that the government had been scrambling to protect.

The second catalyst is the rupee's recovery. After plunging to a record low near 97 per dollar in May, the currency has clawed back to 94.66, aided by a salvo of Reserve Bank of India measures: a subsidised forex swap facility for banks, permission to lend to non-residents against foreign-currency deposits, and the scrapping of capital gains and withholding taxes on government bonds.

> The combination of lower crude, rupee stability, and measures to draw foreign inflows has improved sentiment and liquidity.

> ""India is among the most oversold markets we track," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which manages about $65 billion."

— Ajit Banerjee, president and chief investment officer at Shriram Life Insurance

The Foreign Money Is Coming Back

Exchange data shows daily selling by global funds has slowed markedly in recent weeks. More strikingly, analysis by Elara Capital reveals that inflows into US-listed India-focused exchange-traded funds turned positive last week for the first time in over a month.

"India is among the most oversold markets we track," said Todd McClone, a portfolio manager at William Blair Investment Management, which manages about $65 billion. "This macro improvement, alongside a more attractive valuation premium, strengthens the case to act."

Average allocations to India among emerging market funds had dropped below 10% in April — the lowest since early 2021, down from a peak of 17.5% in August 2024, according to Copley Fund Research. Now, with valuations in high-tech stocks showing signs of excess and India's macro picture brightening, fund managers are reassessing.

Goldman Sachs has raised its 2026 growth forecast for India by 30 basis points, lowered its inflation projection by 20 bps, and now expects a balance of payments surplus of 0.7% of GDP.

Risks Still Lurk

Not everything is settled. The US-Iran peace talks in Doha showed little headway this week, and any renewed escalation could send oil prices spiking again. The monsoon remains a concern — June was the fifth-driest on record, and July rainfall is forecast below the long-period average. A weak monsoon would hurt rural demand and the agricultural sector that employs nearly half the country.

The Federal Reserve is also a wildcard. US inflation remains sticky, and markets see a roughly 50% chance of a rate hike in September. Higher US rates would strengthen the dollar and could trigger fresh outflows from emerging markets, including India.

Despite these risks, the sheer scale of the reversal — from a panicked flight of nearly $27 billion in foreign portfolio outflows this year to tentative re-entry — marks a turning point.

What This Means for NRIs

For diaspora investors with exposure to Indian equities, the $5 trillion milestone validates a thesis that had been badly shaken: that India's structural growth story can absorb external shocks and come back stronger. Those who stayed invested through the May rout are sitting on significant recovery gains. Those who had moved to the sidelines now face a decision about whether the easy money has already been made — or whether the $5 trillion floor is just the beginning of the next leg up.

Sources: Reuters, The Indian Eye, Goldman Sachs Research, Elara Capital, Copley Fund Research, Reserve Bank of India
